question:
A number-pairing rule on the natural numbers is defined by a function $f:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$ such that $f(n)=n+1$ when $n$ is odd and $f(n)=n-1$ when $n$ is even. Thus the rule pairs consecutive natural numbers: $1$ is paired with $2$, $2$ with $1$, $3$ with $4$, $4$ with $3$, and so on. Students investigate whether this rule loses any information about the original input and whether every natural number appears as an output. They must consider odd and even cases carefully rather than relying only on the first few values.

(a) Find $f(7)$, $f(12)$ and $f(21)$.

(b) Show that an odd input and an even input cannot have the same image under $f$.

(c) Prove that $f$ is one-one.

(d) Show that every natural number has a pre-image and hence determine whether $f$ is onto.
explanation:
(a)
Since $7$ is odd, $f(7)=7+1=8$. Since $12$ is even, $f(12)=12-1=11$. Since $21$ is odd, $f(21)=21+1=22$.

(b)
Let $n_1$ be odd and $n_2$ be even. If their images were equal, then $n_1+1=n_2-1$, which gives $n_2-n_1=2$. But the difference between an even integer and an odd integer is odd, whereas $2$ is even. This is impossible. Hence an odd input and an even input cannot have the same image.

(c)
Suppose $f(n_1)=f(n_2)$. By part (b), $n_1$ and $n_2$ must have the same parity. If both are odd, then $n_1+1=n_2+1$, so $n_1=n_2$. If both are even, then $n_1-1=n_2-1$, again giving $n_1=n_2$. Hence, $f$ is one-one.

(d)
Let $y\in\mathbb{N}$. If $y$ is even, then $y-1$ is odd and $f(y-1)=(y-1)+1=y$. If $y$ is odd, then $y+1$ is even and $f(y+1)=(y+1)-1=y$. Thus every natural number has a pre-image. Therefore, $f$ is onto.

options.A: $f(7)=6$, $f(12)=13$ and $f(21)=20$; odd and even inputs can have the same image, so $f$ is neither one-one nor onto.
options.B: $f(7)=8$, $f(12)=11$ and $f(21)=22$; $f$ is one-one but not onto because $1$ has no pre-image.
options.C: $f(7)=8$, $f(12)=11$ and $f(21)=22$; odd and even inputs cannot have the same image, and $f$ is both one-one and onto.
options.D: $f(7)=8$, $f(12)=13$ and $f(21)=22$; $f$ is onto but not one-one because consecutive natural numbers have the same image.
